c.tagline: Where the White Nile meets the world's youngest capital.

taxi.fareNote: No meters; agree the fare with the driver (or boda-boda rider) before departing. Hotels can arrange trusted drivers.

emergency.note: Emergency response is unreliable outside central Juba; most hotels and NGOs keep private security/medevac contacts. Juba Teaching Hospital is the main public facility; serious cases are often evacuated to Nairobi.

avoid.reason: Avoid moving anywhere outside central Juba after dark, and stay away from military installations, checkpoints and the city outskirts, where armed crime and unpredictable security incidents are a serious risk.
Armed robbery and carjacking occur even by day, and photographing officials, infrastructure or checkpoints can lead to detention — travel with an experienced local driver and keep a low profile.

hood_desc: Central commercial and government district with markets, ministries and the main hotels; convenient but busy, noisy and higher risk of petty crime after dark - suits business travelers who want everything walkable.

Leafy Nile-side district housing embassies, UN agencies and NGOs, with the city's most secure upscale hotels and river-view compounds - suits diplomats, aid workers and travelers prioritizing security and comfort.
Working-class residential area west of downtown with guesthouses and local markets at more affordable rates - suits budget travelers and longer-stay visitors wanting an authentic, lower-cost base.
Quieter residential neighborhood near the University of Juba, popular with students, researchers and NGO staff - suits those wanting a calmer, local-feel stay a short ride from the center.
Spacious, green residential area anchored by the Nyakuron Cultural Centre, with compound-style lodging and gardens - suits families, longer-term stays and travelers wanting more room and quiet.

water.note: Tap water is not safe for visitors; use bottled or treated water only.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (South Sudanese pounds) directly to the driver or conductor; there is no fare card or app-based payment system. Matatu fares are fixed per route but not posted, so ask locals or hotel staff the going rate before boarding. Boda-boda and taxi fares must be negotiated before the ride begins.
transit.hours: Public transport generally stops by early evening; a curfew or reduced movement after dark is common, so travel is discouraged at night.
transit.note: There is no formal metro, tram or rail system; matatus and boda-bodas cover most routes, and private/hotel-arranged vehicles are preferred by visitors.

bus: Cross-border coaches to Nairobi, Kampala and Nimule
ferry: Seasonal Nile barge/ferry services (cargo-oriented, limited passenger use)

tip.r: Not deeply ingrained but appreciated at upscale hotels and restaurants catering to expats; round up or leave 5-10% for good service.

food.name: Kisra
food.desc: Paper-thin fermented sorghum flatbread cooked on a hot metal plate, torn and used to scoop up stews; the everyday staple across South Sudan.

places.name: Konyokonyo Market
places.note: Juba's biggest market; the south side is where kisra is flipped on metal plates each morning.

places.name: Lotus Restaurant
places.note: One of the few sit-down places with a proper South Sudanese menu of kisra, asida and stews.

places.name: Custom Market food stalls
places.note: Cluster of cheap cooked-food stalls serving kisra with goat or bean stew all day.

food.name: Ful Medames
food.desc: Slow-cooked fava beans mashed with oil, cumin and lime, topped with white cheese, onion and chilli and eaten with bread; the standard Juba breakfast.

places.name: Konyokonyo Market
places.note: Morning ful carts operate from dawn beside the bread and tea sellers.

places.name: Custom Market food stalls
places.note: Ful carts and tea stands ring the market; the busiest breakfast trade in town.

places.name: Jebel Market
places.note: Neighbourhood market with Sudanese-style bean and bread stalls.

food.name: Charcoal-Grilled Goat
food.desc: Goat ribs and shoulder rubbed with salt and chilli and grilled over charcoal, served on a shared tray with kisra, raw onion and lime.

places.name: Custom Market grills
places.note: Rows of open charcoal grills; a plate of goat with kisra costs about a bus fare.

places.name: Afex Riverside Restaurant
places.note: Long-running expat compound restaurant with a shaded Nile-side terrace and grill.

places.name: Notos Lounge
places.note: Established Juba restaurant and bar with grilled meats and a garden setting.

food.name: Asida with Mullah Stew
food.desc: Smooth sorghum or maize porridge served in a mound with a well of mullah, an okra or dried-meat stew soured with tamarind and thickened with peanut.

places.name: Lotus Restaurant
places.note: Reliable place to find asida and traditional stews cooked properly rather than as a novelty.

places.name: Konyokonyo Market cooked-food stalls
places.note: Women's kitchens inside the market serve asida and stew at lunchtime.

places.name: Quality Hotel Juba
places.note: Hotel restaurant that keeps South Sudanese dishes on the menu alongside international food.

food.name: Grilled Nile Perch and Tilapia
food.desc: Fish pulled from the White Nile, scored, marinated and grilled whole over coals, served with lime, chilli and either kisra or chips.

places.name: Afex Riverside Restaurant
places.note: The classic Nile-side terrace for grilled perch; a Juba fixture for two decades.

places.name: Da Vinci Restaurant
places.note: Long-established riverside restaurant popular for whole grilled fish.

places.name: Logali House
places.note: Well-known hotel courtyard restaurant and one of the safest bets for a sit-down dinner.

food.name: Kajaik
food.desc: Dried or smoked Nile fish simmered into a thick stew with okra, peanut paste and onions; a Dinka and Nuer dish now common on Juba tables.

places.name: Lotus Restaurant
places.note: Serves the traditional dried-fish and peanut stews that are hard to find in hotel kitchens.

places.name: Konyokonyo Market cooked-food stalls
places.note: Market kitchens cook it daily; the dried fish is sold in the same aisles.

places.name: Custom Market food stalls
places.note: Cheap home-style plates of stew and kisra through the middle of the day.

food.name: Sudanese Spiced Tea and Jebena Coffee
food.desc: Sweet black tea with ginger, cardamom or mint, and cardamom coffee poured from a clay jebena pot by the tea ladies who anchor every street corner.

places.name: Hai Cinema tea stands
places.note: Jasmine-scented tea stands under the trees; Juba's default meeting spot.

places.name: Konyokonyo Market
places.note: Tea ladies with low stools and charcoal braziers work every entrance.

places.name: Logali House
places.note: Shaded courtyard for spiced tea and coffee if you want a quieter table.

food.name: Karkade
food.desc: Deep red hibiscus infusion served iced and heavily sweetened, sometimes with ginger or cloves; the standard non-alcoholic drink in the heat.

places.name: Konyokonyo Market
places.note: Dried hibiscus is sold by the sack here and brewed fresh at the drink stalls.

places.name: Custom Market food stalls
places.note: Cold karkade and tamarind juice sold from coolers beside the grills.

places.name: Quality Hotel Juba
places.note: Hotel bar and restaurant serving chilled karkade and fresh juices.

landmarks: Dr. John Garang Mausoleum
The final resting place of South Sudan's founding hero draws visitors and pilgrims alike, standing as the most solemn and significant monument in the young nation's capital.
Juba Bridge (Freedom Bridge)
The only bridge spanning the White Nile in Juba, this steel crossing offers sweeping river views and is a key gateway symbolizing the city's connection to the storied river.
White Nile Riverfront
Watching the White Nile flow past Juba at sunset, often from a riverside restaurant or boat, is one of the most memorable and photographed experiences in the city.
Kator Church (St. Theresa Cathedral)
This historic Catholic cathedral in the Kator district serves as a spiritual anchor for Juba's Christian community and a landmark of the city's colonial-era religious architecture.
All Saints Cathedral
The Episcopal cathedral of Juba stands as a striking example of modern ecclesiastical architecture and a gathering point for the city's Anglican congregation.
Jebel Kujur
This rocky hill rising over Juba's western edge offers panoramic views across the city and the Nile valley, making it a favorite spot for hikers and photographers.
University of Juba
As South Sudan's leading institution of higher learning, the university's campus is a point of national pride and a symbol of the country's investment in its future.
Konyo Konyo Market
Juba's largest and busiest market bursts with traders, fresh produce, and textiles, offering visitors an authentic and colorful immersion into local commerce and daily life.
Nyakuron Cultural Centre
This open-air venue hosts traditional dance, music performances, and cultural festivals, making it the best place to experience South Sudan's diverse ethnic heritage firsthand.
Custom Market
A sprawling riverside trading hub near the Nile, this market is known for its bustling atmosphere, imported goods, and glimpse into Juba's commercial lifeblood.

train.note: South Sudan has no railway serving Juba (a short freight stub reaches only Wau in the north). Long-distance travel is by road or air.

bus.note: The busy overland route is Juba-Kampala (roughly a day) crossing at Nimule. Bebeto Coach is one operator with online booking; others such as Nile Star, Gateway and Kampala Coach run the route too but mostly take bookings in person or via Facebook. Buses go from the Konyo Konyo/Custom area; carry a Ugandan visa or East Africa documents. Security on stretches of the road varies - check current advice.

ferry.note: No international ferries. Barge traffic on the White Nile (Juba toward Kosti/Malakal) is domestic, seasonal and heavily disrupted by conflict - not a dependable passenger option.
